clue.text: I These plains are very plain, even to a Bolshevik.

definitions.text: These plains are very plain, even to a Bolshevik

parts.note: the surface reading: some landscape so flat and featureless that anyone would notice
the setter's reading: the plains are Russian ones, so a Bolshevik knows them as home ground

explanation.surface: A Russian revolutionary finds even his own flat countryside dull.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'plain' plays flat land against the adjective for unadorned; the Bolshevik places the plains in Russia.
explanation.definitionFit: The steppes are the vast treeless grasslands stretching across southern Russia and Central Asia.

clue.text: Train with a gold coin in it.

definitions.text: Train with a gold coin in it

parts.note: the setter's reading: to teach or school, not a railway train

parts.words: with a gold coin in it
parts.note: the setter's reading: the word for train holds the name of an old Venetian gold coin among its letters

explanation.surface: A railway train with a gold coin left on board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' is the meaning; the rest observes that the answer has the ducat, an old European gold coin, inside it, but its outer letters are not clued.
explanation.definitionFit: To educate is to train or teach, especially to give someone schooling.

definitions.text: Possibly a William

parts.note: the setter's reading: this is one example of a kind
the surface reading: a man called William; the setter means the Williams variety of fruit

explanation.surface: Guessing that some man might be named William.
explanation.walkthrough: The Williams (Bon Chrétien) is a well-known variety of this fruit, so a William is one example of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Williams is a popular variety of the sweet juicy orchard fruit, also called Bartlett.

clue.text: The King's variety wear silk robes.

definitions.text: The King's variety wear silk robes

parts.note: the surface reading: a royal kind of something, perhaps a fabric or plant
the setter's reading: senior barristers appointed by the Crown wear silk gowns in court, hence 'taking silk'

explanation.surface: Royalty's own kind of people dress in silken gowns.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a senior barrister appointed King's (now King's or Queen's) Counsel is said to 'take silk', from the silk gown worn in court.
explanation.definitionFit: King's Counsel is one variety of legal adviser or barrister, the senior rank wearing silk gowns.

clue.text: This beat Napoleon hollow at Waterloo.

definitions.text: This beat Napoleon hollow at Waterloo

parts.note: the surface reading: some general or army that thrashed the French emperor
the setter's reading seems to be the British infantry formed in hollow squares, which the French cavalry could not break

explanation.surface: A history-book line about who defeated Napoleon in 1815.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is confirmed by the solution printed the next day, but the link is unclear: the likeliest one is the hollow squares the British infantry formed at Waterloo, with the setter stretching square into its solid form.
explanation.definitionFit: A cube is the solid with six square faces, the three-dimensional square, so it loosely stands for the infantry formation.

clue.text: Buffalo Bill had his fling with these.

definitions.text: Buffalo Bill had his fling with these

parts.note: the surface reading: the showman enjoyed a wild spell or romance
the setter's reading: fling means throw, and a cowboy throws a looped rope

explanation.surface: The Wild West showman's fling with some unnamed partners.
explanation.walkthrough: Buffalo Bill Cody ran a touring Wild West show; 'fling' means a literal throw of a rope noose.
explanation.definitionFit: Lassoes are long ropes with running nooses that cowboys throw to catch cattle.

clue.text: A military expedition which never appealed to the Turks.

definitions.text: A military expedition which never appealed to the Turks

parts.note: the surface reading: any armed campaign

parts.words: which never appealed to the Turks
parts.note: the setter's reading: the medieval Christian campaigns to take the Holy Land were fought against Muslim Turks

explanation.surface: An understated remark that some army campaign was unpopular in Turkey.
explanation.walkthrough: The understatement points to the medieval wars fought by Christian Europe against the Seljuk and other Turkish rulers of the Holy Land.
explanation.definitionFit: A crusade was a medieval Christian military campaign to win Jerusalem and the Holy Land.

clue.text: These always have to take advantage of Hobson's choice.

definitions.text: These always have to take advantage of Hobson's choice

parts.note: the surface reading: some group forced to accept whatever is offered
the setter's reading: Hobson's choice is no choice at all, and the proverb says these people can't be choosers

explanation.surface: Some people are always stuck taking what they are offered.
explanation.walkthrough: Hobson's choice, from a Cambridge stable owner who let you take the horse nearest the door or none, means no real choice; the proverb 'beggars can't be choosers' supplies the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: People who ask alms must accept whatever is given them, as the proverb about choosers says.

clue.text: A tooth process, but not dentistry.

definitions.text: A tooth process, but not dentistry

parts.note: the surface reading: a dental procedure such as filling or extraction
the setter's reading: something one does with one's own teeth, in rage or pain

explanation.surface: Something done to teeth that a dentist has no part in.
explanation.definitionFit: To gnash is to grind the teeth together, a sign of anger or anguish.

clue.text: You have left something out? Well, put this in.

definitions.text: You have left something out? Well, put this in

parts.note: the surface reading: a forgetful person is told to add whatever they missed
the setter's reading: the mark a writer or proofreader inserts to show where omitted words go

explanation.surface: Someone forgot an item and is told simply to add it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This' is not the missing thing itself but the mark that shows where it belongs.
explanation.definitionFit: A caret is the small inverted-V proofreading mark placed below a line to show an insertion.

clue.text: This happens and surely interests someone.

definitions.text: This happens and surely interests someone

parts.note: the setter's reading: an occurrence, something that takes place
the surface reading: a vague remark that anything going on will catch somebody's attention

explanation.surface: A shrug: whatever goes on, somebody will care.
explanation.definitionFit: An event is any occurrence, especially a notable one that draws attention or an audience.

clue.text: A boast, that's very like poker.

definitions.text: A boast
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a piece of bragging talk

definitions.text: that's very like poker
definitions.meaning: second meaning: an old three-card game from which poker descends

explanation.surface: Bragging, says the speaker, is much like a poker bluff.
explanation.walkthrough: Brag is a British card game, still played, with betting and bluffing much as in poker.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a noun for boastful talk and the name of a bluffing card game for gamblers.

definitions.text: Cricketing pedlar

parts.note: the setter's first reading: the surname of England's cricket captain when this puzzle appeared
the setter's second reading: an old word for a travelling hawker of goods

explanation.surface: A hawker who also plays cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: A. P. F. Chapman captained England in 1926-30; his surname is also an archaic word for a pedlar.
explanation.definitionFit: A chapman was an itinerant dealer selling small goods, the historical word for a hawker.

clue.text: If it were mobile you might tour with it.

definitions.text: If it were mobile you might tour with it

parts.note: the surface reading: something that can be moved about
the setter's reading: add the word mobile to the answer and you get a motor car to tour in

explanation.surface: Musing that some object would be good for touring if only it could move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile' is to be tacked onto the answer: the prefix plus mobile makes the motor car.
explanation.definitionFit: Auto is the prefix meaning self, which with mobile forms the old word for a motor car.

clue.text: He is never satis-fied with the rate of exchange.

definitions.text: He is never satis-fied with the rate of exchange

parts.note: the surface reading: a discontented money-changer or traveller
the setter's reading: the exchange is a telephone exchange, and the rate is how fast calls go through

explanation.surface: A grumbler forever complaining about currency rates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rate of exchange' suggests foreign money, but it means the speed of a telephone exchange, where this operator connected calls.
explanation.definitionFit: A telephonist was the operator who connected callers by hand at a telephone switchboard.

definitions.text: Ten for each of us

parts.note: the surface reading: a share of ten things handed out
the setter's reading: every person has ten of these, on the feet

explanation.surface: Sharing out: ten apiece.
explanation.walkthrough: Fingers come to mind first, but they number eight plus two thumbs; the feet give ten digits.
explanation.definitionFit: Toes are the digits of the foot, five on each, so ten per person.

definitions.text: Layers

parts.note: the surface reading: strata or coats, pronounced to rhyme with players
the setter's reading: things that lay, as birds lay eggs

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'layers' as 'those who lay': farmyard birds kept for eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: Hens are female domestic fowl kept by farmers to lay eggs.

clue.text: Not necessarily of the peerage, but a peer probably of the same age.

definitions.text: Not necessarily of the peerage, but a peer probably of the same age

parts.note: the surface reading: peer as a lord, which this is not

parts.words: but a peer probably of the same age
parts.note: the setter's reading: peer as an equal, a companion of like standing

explanation.surface: A careful distinction between a lord and someone's equal in years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peerage' sends the mind to the House of Lords; the peer here is simply an equal or comrade.
explanation.definitionFit: A compeer is an equal in rank or ability, a companion or associate, often a contemporary.

clue.text: Process common to music, hearts and policemen.

definitions.text: Process common to music, hearts and policemen

parts.note: the surface reading: a single procedure shared by three unlike things
the setter's reading: music keeps time to it, hearts do it, and a constable walks one

explanation.surface: A riddle asking what links a song, a pulse and a bobby.
explanation.walkthrough: A policeman's regular patrol route is his beat; music's pulse and the heart's throb are the other two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means rhythmic pulse in music, a heart's throb, and a constable's patrol round.

clue.text: You will need something like a crane to get this.

definitions.text: You will need something like a crane to get this

parts.words: You will need something like a crane
parts.note: the surface reading: lifting machinery for a heavy load
the setter's reading: the answer is itself something like a crane, a big long-legged bird

explanation.surface: Heavy lifting gear is required for some bulky object.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crane' suggests a machine; it is the bird, and the answer is a large crane-like game bird of open plains.
explanation.definitionFit: The bustard is a heavy long-legged bird of open country, related to and resembling the crane.

definitions.text: Sometimes given the boot

parts.note: the surface reading: occasionally sacked or kicked out
the setter's reading: a cloth gaiter is sometimes buttoned over a man's boot or shoe

explanation.surface: Someone who gets dismissed now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Given the boot' means sacked; here it is literal: a short cloth covering fastened over the instep and ankle, fashionable when this puzzle appeared.
explanation.definitionFit: A spat is a short gaiter worn over the instep and ankle, covering the top of a shoe.

definitions.text: This will want dressing

parts.note: the surface reading: someone or something lacking
the setter's reading: oil and vinegar poured over greens, not clothes or bandages

explanation.surface: Something that still needs clothes or a bandage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dressing' suggests clothes or a wound dressing; it is the sauce poured over leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A salad of raw leaves is usually served with a dressing such as vinaigrette.

definitions.text: Four to a company

parts.note: the surface reading: a number, as in a party of four
the setter's reading: an army company was divided into four of these sub-units

explanation.surface: A small group of four makes company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Company' suggests friends; it is the army unit, which in the British Army of the time had four of these.
explanation.definitionFit: A platoon is a military sub-unit, several of which make up an infantry company.

clue.text: This describes the science of the correct use of language.

definitions.text: This describes the science of the correct use of language

parts.note: the setter's reading: the answer is an adjective, a describing word

parts.words: the science of the correct use of language
parts.note: the surface reading: a definition of linguistics or grammar itself

explanation.surface: A schoolroom definition of a branch of language study.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as defining a noun, but 'describes' asks for the adjective that goes with it.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammatical is the adjective relating to grammar, the rules for correct sentences.

clue.text: It sounds sluggish but try it with gin

definitions.text: try it with gin

indicators.note: says the answer is heard as the next word when spoken, not spelt like it

parts.note: sluggish means slow, said the same as the blackthorn fruit

explanation.surface: Something seems dull, but try mixing it with gin.
explanation.walkthrough: Sloe gin is a liqueur made by steeping the sour blackthorn berries in gin.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloes are the small sour blackthorn fruits steeped in gin to make a liqueur.

definitions.text: A sleepy
definitions.note: an adjective phrase standing for the noun: sleepy things

indicators.note: something going backward runs in the opposite direction, so the word is read from its end

parts.note: a span is a bridge or the stretch it crosses

explanation.surface: A drowsy person walking backwards over a road.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: sleepy here stands for short sleeps.
explanation.definitionFit: Naps are short sleeps, what a drowsy person takes during the day.

definitions.text: These cool bearings

parts.note: the surface reading: something calm or fashionable
the setter's reading: the machine parts in which shafts turn, kept from overheating by lubrication

explanation.surface: Something that steadies one's composure or sense of direction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bearings' suggests direction-finding or demeanour; it is the machine part, cooled by lubricants.
explanation.definitionFit: Lubricating fluids reduce friction in machinery, keeping moving bearings from overheating.

definitions.text: I do, sire (anag.)
definitions.note: the clue has no definition: it is the anagram fodder and its label alone

indicators.note: the setter's plain label telling the solver to rearrange the preceding words

parts.note: the words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A courtier's reply of assent to the king.
explanation.walkthrough: Early Times puzzles gave some anagrams with no definition at all, just the label; the answer is a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Isidore is a man's given name, borne by Saint Isidore of Seville among others.

clue.text: Found in the kitchen or the theatre.

definitions.text: Found in the kitchen or the theatre

parts.note: one reading: a sideboard with shelves for plates
the other reading: a person who helps actors into their costumes

explanation.surface: A puzzle about something at home both by the stove and backstage.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a kitchen cupboard with plate shelves and a backstage costume assistant.

clue.text: The results of backing slow horses.

definitions.text: The results of backing slow horses

parts.note: the surface reading: perhaps reversing horses, or supporting them
the setter's reading: backing means betting on, and slow runners lose

explanation.surface: What a punter gets for betting on the wrong nags.
explanation.definitionFit: Losings are the sums lost, here in wagers on racehorses that finished out of the money.
